title: The Collective Intelligence of Groups
text:
Psychologists have long known that a person who does well on one kind of mental test tends to do well on others, the pattern behind the idea of general intelligence. In 2010, Anita Woolley, Christopher Chabris, Alex Pentland, Nada Hashmi and Thomas Malone, working at Carnegie Mellon, MIT and Union College, asked whether groups show something similar.

They brought hundreds of people into the lab in small groups and gave each group a range of tasks: brainstorming, solving visual puzzles, negotiating over limited resources, making moral judgments and planning a shopping trip, among others. Groups that did well on one task tended to do well on the others, suggesting a general factor the authors called collective intelligence.

What predicted it was not mainly the average intelligence of the members or the score of the smartest person. Groups did better when members took turns more evenly instead of being dominated by one or two speakers, and when members scored higher on a test of reading emotions from pictures of people's eyes. Groups with a larger share of women also did better, which the authors linked to the women's higher average scores on that social sensitivity test.
lesson: A team of bright people is not automatically a bright team. Share the airtime and pay attention to how others are feeling, and the whole group thinks better.
people: Anita Woolley, Christopher Chabris, Alex Pentland, Nada Hashmi, Thomas Malone
location: Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, and MIT, Cambridge, USA
source: Woolley, A. W., Chabris, C. F., Pentland, A., Hashmi, N., and Malone, T. W. (2010). Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups. Science, 330(6004), 686-688.
caveat: Later reanalyses and studies have debated how strong and general the collective intelligence factor is.
